subject: biology
title: Ageing and cell death
summary: Compares apoptosis with necrosis and explains the caspase pathways of apoptosis, telomere shortening and cellular senescence, the main theories of ageing, and cancer as a loss of control over division and death.
body:
Cells do not live forever, and that is often a good thing. Your fingers separated before birth because the cells between them died on cue, and millions of your cells die every day so that damaged or unneeded cells do not build up. When cells die at the wrong time, or fail to die when they should, the result can be disease: too much death contributes to neurodegeneration, too little to cancer. This lesson looks at how cells die, why they age, and how cancer cells escape both limits.

## Key ideas

### Two ways for a cell to die

**Apoptosis** is **programmed cell death**: an orderly, energy-requiring process the cell carries out itself. **Necrosis** is uncontrolled death caused by severe injury such as loss of blood supply, toxins, burns or physical trauma.

| Feature | Apoptosis | Necrosis |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | Internal or external signals; normal development or damage | Severe injury (e.g. lack of oxygen, toxins) |
| Energy | Needs ATP | Often follows ATP loss |
| Cell size | Shrinks | Swells |
| Membrane | Stays intact; forms blebs | Ruptures |
| Nucleus | Chromatin condenses, DNA cut into regular fragments | Breaks down irregularly |
| Contents | Packaged into **apoptotic bodies** | Spill out into tissue |
| Inflammation | None | Yes |
| Number of cells | Usually single cells | Often groups of cells |

The key difference for the body is inflammation. Apoptotic cells expose the phospholipid **phosphatidylserine** on the outer face of their membrane (it is normally kept on the inner face), which acts as an "eat me" signal. **Phagocytes** such as macrophages quickly engulf the apoptotic bodies, so nothing leaks out. In necrosis, released contents trigger inflammation, which can damage neighbouring tissue.

### Why apoptosis matters

- **Development** — removing the webbing between fingers and toes, and pruning excess neurones.
- **Immune system** — removing T cells that would attack the body's own tissues, and killing virus-infected cells.
- **Tissue maintenance** — balancing cell division so organs stay the right size.
- **Protection** — eliminating cells with DNA damage that cannot be repaired.

### How apoptosis works: caspases

Apoptosis is carried out by **caspases**, protease enzymes that cut target proteins at specific sites. They exist as inactive precursors (**procaspases**). **Initiator caspases** are activated first; they cut and activate **executioner caspases**, which in turn cut hundreds of cellular proteins. This cascade amplifies the signal and makes the decision irreversible. Executioner caspases dismantle the cytoskeleton and nuclear lamina, and activate an enzyme that cuts DNA between nucleosomes, giving DNA fragments in multiples of about 180–200 base pairs (a "DNA ladder" on a gel).

There are two main pathways:

**1. Extrinsic (death receptor) pathway.** A signal molecule from another cell, such as **Fas ligand** on a cytotoxic T cell, binds a **death receptor** (such as Fas) on the target cell's surface. The receptors cluster and recruit adaptor proteins, which activate **caspase-8**, an initiator caspase.

**2. Intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway.** Internal stress, such as DNA damage detected by **p53**, loss of survival signals or oxidative stress, changes the balance of the **Bcl-2 family** of proteins. **Pro-apoptotic** members (such as Bax and Bak) make the outer mitochondrial membrane permeable; **anti-apoptotic** members (such as Bcl-2 itself) block this. When pro-apoptotic signals win, **cytochrome c** is released from the mitochondrial intermembrane space into the cytosol. There it binds the adaptor protein Apaf-1 to form the **apoptosome**, which activates **caspase-9**.

Both pathways converge on executioner caspases such as **caspase-3**.

### Telomeres and the end-replication problem

**Telomeres** are repeated DNA sequences at the ends of linear chromosomes (in humans the repeat is TTAGGG, repeated thousands of times), bound by protective proteins. They stop chromosome ends from being mistaken for broken DNA and joined together.

DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to an existing 3′ end and needs an RNA primer to start. On the lagging strand, when the last primer at the very end of the chromosome is removed, there is nothing upstream for DNA polymerase to extend from, so the gap cannot be filled. This is the **end-replication problem**, and it means telomeres shorten a little with each round of replication.

The enzyme **telomerase** solves this. It is a **reverse transcriptase** that carries its own RNA template and uses it to add telomere repeats to the 3′ end. Telomerase is active in germ-line cells, many stem cells and most cancer cells, but is low or absent in most somatic cells.

### Cellular senescence

In the 1960s, Leonard Hayflick showed that normal human cells grown in culture divide only a limited number of times before stopping; this is the **Hayflick limit**. We now know one major cause is telomere shortening: when telomeres become critically short, the cell detects them as DNA damage, p53 is activated and the cell enters **replicative senescence**, a permanent arrest of division. Senescence can also be triggered early by other stresses, such as oncogene activation or DNA damage.

Senescent cells are alive and metabolically active but no longer divide. They are often larger and flatter, and many release a mix of inflammatory signals, growth factors and enzymes. This **senescence-associated secretory phenotype** may harm surrounding tissue as senescent cells accumulate with age.

Senescence is a double-edged sword: it acts as a barrier against cancer by stopping damaged cells dividing, but the build-up of senescent cells may contribute to ageing.

### Theories of ageing

**Ageing** is the gradual decline in function of cells, tissues and organisms over time, increasing the risk of disease and death. No single cause explains it; the theories below are not mutually exclusive.

- **Telomere theory** — progressive telomere shortening limits cell division and tissue renewal.
- **Free radical (oxidative damage) theory** — **reactive oxygen species (ROS)**, by-products of the mitochondrial electron transport chain, damage DNA, proteins and lipids. Damage builds up over time; mitochondrial DNA is especially exposed because it is close to the source.
- **DNA damage and mutation accumulation** — repair is imperfect, so mutations accumulate in somatic cells, disrupting function.
- **Programmed (genetic) theories** — lifespan is influenced by genes and signalling pathways. In model organisms such as nematode worms, mutations in some nutrient-sensing pathways (such as the insulin/IGF-1 pathway) extend lifespan.
- **Evolutionary theories** — natural selection is weak on traits that act after reproduction, so harmful late-acting alleles are not removed, and genes that help early reproduction may be favoured even if they cause damage later.

### Cancer as loss of control

**Cancer** is uncontrolled cell division caused by accumulated mutations, typically in two classes of genes:

- **Proto-oncogenes** promote division (for example, growth factor receptors and the signalling protein Ras). A mutation that makes them overactive turns them into **oncogenes**. One mutated copy is usually enough (a dominant, gain-of-function effect), acting like a stuck accelerator.
- **Tumour suppressor genes** inhibit division or trigger apoptosis (for example, *TP53* and *RB1*). Both copies usually need to be inactivated (a recessive, loss-of-function effect), like failed brakes. This is the basis of the **two-hit hypothesis**.

Cancer cells gain a set of abilities: they divide without growth signals, ignore stop signals, **evade apoptosis** (for example, by overproducing Bcl-2 or losing p53), achieve **replicative immortality** (usually by switching telomerase back on), grow new blood vessels to supply the tumour, and eventually invade other tissues (**metastasis**). Because several mutations are usually needed, cancer risk rises with age.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: distinguishing apoptosis from necrosis

A tissue sample from a heart attack shows swollen cells with burst membranes and many white blood cells. A sample from a developing mouse paw shows isolated shrunken cells with condensed nuclei, surrounded by macrophages but no inflammation.

1. Heart: swelling, ruptured membranes and inflammation indicate **necrosis**, consistent with oxygen loss from a blocked artery.
2. Paw: single shrunken cells with condensed chromatin and no inflammation indicate **apoptosis**, consistent with removal of the webbing between digits.

### Example 2: interpreting a DNA gel

DNA from three cell samples is run on a gel. Sample P shows a ladder of bands at about 200, 400, 600 and 800 base pairs. Sample Q shows a continuous smear. Sample R shows one band of very high molecular weight.

- P: regular fragments in multiples of about 200 bp show cutting between nucleosomes, which is characteristic of **apoptosis**.
- Q: random fragments give a smear, characteristic of **necrosis**.
- R: intact DNA indicates **healthy cells**.

### Example 3: telomere data

Fibroblasts are grown in culture. At population doubling 10 their average telomere length is 9 kb; at doubling 40 it is 6 kb.

1. Loss = 9 − 6 = 3 kb over 30 doublings.
2. Rate = 3000 bp ÷ 30 = **100 bp per doubling**.
3. If cells senesce at about 4 kb, they have 6 − 4 = 2 kb left, which is 2000 ÷ 100 = **about 20 more doublings**.
4. If the cells are engineered to express telomerase, telomere length would be maintained and they would keep dividing beyond this point.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking apoptosis is always harmful. It is essential for normal development and protection against cancer.
- Saying necrosis needs energy or follows a program. Apoptosis is the energy-requiring, controlled process.
- Describing senescent cells as dead. They are alive but permanently stopped dividing.
- Saying telomerase is active in all cells. It is active mainly in germ-line, stem and cancer cells.
- Treating oncogenes and tumour suppressors as the same. Oncogenes are gain-of-function (usually one hit); tumour suppressors are loss-of-function (usually two hits).

## Exam tips

- When comparing apoptosis and necrosis, give paired features (shrink versus swell, no inflammation versus inflammation) rather than describing each separately.
- For pathway questions, name the trigger, the key molecules and the final effector (for example, DNA damage → p53 → Bax → cytochrome c → apoptosome → caspase-9 → caspase-3).
- Data questions on telomere length or cell doublings often require a simple rate calculation; show the subtraction and division.
- Link cancer to earlier lessons: checkpoints, p53 and Rb from the cell cycle, and telomerase from DNA replication.

## Tips to remember

- **Apoptosis is a planned demolition; necrosis is a building collapse**: apoptosis is quiet and tidy (cell shrinks, contents packed into apoptotic bodies, no inflammation); necrosis is messy (cell swells, membrane bursts, contents spill, inflammation).
- **"Shrink and pack" vs "swell and burst"** (made-up memory trick): if a question describes a cell, ask yourself which pair of words fits. That one check sorts most apoptosis/necrosis questions.
- **"8 from outside, 9 from inside, both meet at 3"** (made-up memory trick): the extrinsic (death receptor) pathway activates caspase-8, the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway activates caspase-9, and both converge on executioner caspase-3.
- **Telomeres are the plastic tips on shoelaces (aglets)**: each round of replication wears a little off (the end-replication problem) until, at a critically short length, the cell treats them as DNA damage and enters senescence. Telomerase is the shop that puts new tips back on, and it is mostly found in germ-line, stem and cancer cells.
- **Accelerator and brakes**: an oncogene is a stuck accelerator (one hit, gain of function); a tumour suppressor such as *TP53* is the brakes, and you have to lose both copies before they fail (two hits, loss of function).
- **Quick self-check**: senescent cells are alive but have permanently stopped dividing. If you wrote "dead", you have mixed them up with apoptosis.

## Key terms

- **Apoptosis** — programmed, controlled cell death without inflammation.
- **Necrosis** — uncontrolled cell death after severe injury, causing inflammation.
- **Caspase** — protease that carries out apoptosis by cutting target proteins.
- **Apoptosome** — complex of cytochrome c and Apaf-1 that activates caspase-9.
- **Bcl-2 family** — proteins that promote or block release of cytochrome c from mitochondria.
- **Telomere** — repeated DNA sequence protecting the end of a linear chromosome.
- **Telomerase** — reverse transcriptase that lengthens telomeres using its own RNA template.
- **Hayflick limit** — limited number of divisions a normal cell can complete in culture.
- **Senescence** — permanent, irreversible arrest of cell division in a living cell.
- **Oncogene** — overactive, mutated version of a gene that promotes cell division.

## Summary

- Apoptosis is orderly and quiet; necrosis is messy and inflammatory.
- Apoptosis is triggered by death receptors (extrinsic) or mitochondrial cytochrome c release (intrinsic); both activate a caspase cascade.
- Telomeres shorten with each division because of the end-replication problem; telomerase can restore them.
- Critically short telomeres trigger senescence, which protects against cancer but may contribute to ageing.
- Ageing has several overlapping causes, including oxidative damage, mutation build-up and telomere loss.
- Cancer results from oncogene activation and tumour suppressor loss, letting cells divide without control, evade apoptosis and become immortal.

questions.prompt: Which feature is characteristic of apoptosis but NOT necrosis?

options.A: The cell swells and its membrane bursts
options.B: Cell contents trigger an inflammatory response
options.C: The cell shrinks and is broken into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies
options.D: It always affects large groups of neighbouring cells

questions.explanation: Apoptotic cells shrink and package their contents into apoptotic bodies that phagocytes engulf. Options A, B and D describe necrosis, with B the most tempting since inflammation is the key clinical difference.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the enzyme telomerase?

options.A: It removes RNA primers from the lagging strand
options.B: It adds repeated DNA sequences to chromosome ends using its own RNA template
options.D: It cuts DNA between nucleosomes during apoptosis

questions.explanation: Telomerase is a reverse transcriptase carrying an RNA template, which it uses to extend telomeres. Option C describes DNA ligase, and A describes the primer removal that actually causes the end-replication problem.

questions.prompt: In the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis, what is the role of cytochrome c released from mitochondria?

options.A: It binds Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome, which activates caspase-9
options.B: It binds death receptors on the cell surface
options.C: It directly digests DNA in the nucleus
options.D: It increases ATP production to fuel cell repair

questions.explanation: In the cytosol, cytochrome c joins Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome, which activates the initiator caspase-9. Option B describes the extrinsic pathway's start, and D confuses its normal role in the electron transport chain with its role in apoptosis.

questions.prompt: Why does the lagging strand of a linear chromosome get shorter with each round of DNA replication?

options.A: DNA polymerase cannot read the TTAGGG sequence
options.B: Helicase cannot unwind the end of the chromosome
options.C: Ligase cannot join the final Okazaki fragment because it is too short
options.D: When the final RNA primer is removed, DNA polymerase has no 3′ end from which to fill the gap

questions.explanation: DNA polymerase can only extend an existing 3′ end. At the very tip of the lagging strand, the gap left by the last primer cannot be filled. Option C is tempting but wrong: the problem is a missing template for extension, not ligation.

questions.prompt: Cancer cells often over-produce the protein Bcl-2. How does this help the cancer to grow?

options.A: Bcl-2 activates caspases, increasing cell turnover
options.B: Bcl-2 blocks release of cytochrome c, so damaged cells avoid apoptosis
options.C: Bcl-2 lengthens telomeres, making the cells immortal
options.D: Bcl-2 is a growth factor that stimulates division

questions.explanation: Bcl-2 is anti-apoptotic: it keeps the outer mitochondrial membrane intact so cytochrome c is not released, letting damaged cells survive. Option C describes telomerase, a different cancer adaptation.

questions.prompt: Why does a mutation in a tumour suppressor gene usually need to affect both alleles before it contributes to cancer, whereas an oncogene mutation usually needs to affect only one?

options.A: Tumour suppressor genes are only on the X chromosome
options.B: Tumour suppressor mutations are always dominant
options.C: One working tumour suppressor allele can still make enough protein to restrain division, whereas one overactive oncogene allele pushes division regardless of the other allele
options.D: Oncogenes are found only in viruses

questions.explanation: Tumour suppressor mutations are loss-of-function and usually recessive at the cell level, so both copies must fail. Oncogenes are gain-of-function, so one overactive copy is enough. Option B reverses this relationship.

questions.prompt: Human fibroblasts have average telomere lengths of 10 kb at population doubling 20 and 7 kb at doubling 50. If the cells senesce when telomeres reach 5 kb, about how many more doublings remain after doubling 50?
questions.explanation: Loss = 3 kb over 30 doublings = 100 bp per doubling. Remaining = 7 − 5 = 2 kb = 2000 bp, so 2000 ÷ 100 = 20 doublings. Option A comes from using all 7 kb as the remaining length instead of stopping at the 5 kb limit.

questions.prompt: DNA extracted from a tissue sample shows a ladder of bands at about 200, 400 and 600 base pairs on a gel. What does this indicate?

options.C: The cells were healthy and dividing

questions.explanation: During apoptosis, an enzyme activated by executioner caspases cuts DNA between nucleosomes, giving fragments in multiples of about 200 bp. Necrosis (B) produces random breakage, which appears as a smear rather than distinct bands.
